title: Suffixes
subtitle: -er, -ee, -ist, -ness, -able
summary: Recognise and use the endings that build English words - -er, -or, -ee, -ist, -ness, -able, -ise and more - and use them to tell a noun from a verb or an adjective.

lesson.heading: -er and -or: the person or thing that does it
lesson.text: **-er** makes a noun out of almost any verb, for the person who does the activity. Sometimes the same suffix is spelt **-or**; it is worth keeping a list of those as you meet them. Both endings are also used for things that do a particular job.

examples.text: people: a **writer**, a **painter**, a **worker**, a **shopper**, a **teacher**
spelt -or: an **actor**, a **donor**, an **operator**, a **sailor**, a **supervisor**
examples.note: a donor is a person who donates something; a supervisor makes sure other people do their jobs correctly

examples.text: things: a pencil **sharpener**, a bottle **opener**, a **grater**, a **projector**, a **stapler**, a coat **hanger**

right.label: -ee: the person who receives or experiences it
examples: the **addressee** is the person a letter is written to
the **payee** is the person the money is paid to

lesson.heading: Noun suffixes
rows: complication, pollution, reduction, alteration, donation, promotion, admission, action
a person: politics, beliefs, profession, musicians
Marxist, typist, physicist, terrorist, pianist, violinist, cellist
goodness, readiness, forgetfulness, happiness, sadness, weakness
lesson.note: Adjectives ending in -y change to -i before -ness: happy becomes happiness, lazy becomes laziness.

lesson.heading: Adjective and verb suffixes
lesson.text: **-able** and **-ible** added to a verb mean 'can be done'. **-ise** (or **-ize**, commoner in American English) makes verbs out of adjectives, and **-ify** also makes verbs.

examples.note: edible = can be eaten; flexible = can be bent
terrify = cause someone to be extremely afraid

lesson.heading: Other suffixes that show the word class
lesson.note: Outrageous means shocking and morally unacceptable; harmless means it cannot hurt or damage anyone.

lesson.heading: Suffixes can move the stress
lesson.text: Adding a suffix sometimes changes where the stress falls in a word, so check in a dictionary when you learn a new form.
The informal suffix *-ish* can go on most common adjectives, ages and times to make them vaguer: *She's thirtyish. He has reddish hair. Come about eightish.*

exercises.prompt: Match each description with the -er / -or object it names.

pairs.left: you use it to fasten sheets of paper together
you hang a jacket on it
it makes a blunt pencil sharp again
it shows a film on a screen
you use it to get into a tin of beans
it wipes rain off your car windscreen

exercises.prompt: Does each word mean a thing, a person, or can it mean both?
A person who plays classical violin is a classical ___.
exercises.explanation: -ist is used for people who play musical instruments: pianist, violinist, cellist.

exercises.prompt: A person to whom a sum of money is paid is a ___.
exercises.explanation: -ee marks the person who receives or experiences the action.

exercises.prompt: A person to whom a letter is addressed is the ___.
exercises.explanation: The sender writes it; the addressee receives it.

exercises.prompt: A person who donates their organs upon their death is an organ ___.
exercises.explanation: Donor is one of the -er words spelt with -or.

exercises.prompt: Most of his crimes can be forgiven. Most of his crimes are ___.
exercises.explanation: -able added to a verb means 'can be done'. Note the dropped e: forgive becomes forgivable.

exercises.prompt: Her only fault is that she is lazy. Her only fault is ___.
exercises.explanation: Adjectives ending in -y change the y to i before -ness.

exercises.prompt: I have lovely memories of when I was a child. I have lovely memories of my ___.
exercises.explanation: -hood forms abstract nouns, especially family terms: childhood, motherhood, brotherhood.

exercises.prompt: The most important thing in life is having friends. The most important thing in life is ___.
exercises.explanation: -ship forms abstract nouns, especially about status and relationships.

exercises.prompt: The Club refuses to admit anyone not wearing shoes. The Club refuses ___ to anyone not wearing shoes.
exercises.explanation: -sion turns the verb admit into the noun admission.

exercises.prompt: This firm has produced a lot recently. This firm has been very ___ recently.
exercises.explanation: -ive makes the adjective; productive means producing a large positive amount.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the verb formed from *modern*?
exercises.explanation: -ise (or -ize in American English) forms verbs from adjectives.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb with the abstract noun formed from it.
What part of speech does each suffix usually make?

exercises.explanation: Correct - -ous makes the adjective: fury becomes furious, meaning very angry.
